say.text: A 35-year-old man has right iliac fossa pain and fever. No child, no pregnancy. Which test is the investigation of choice?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Set aside the test you remember from past papers. Which one is most accurate in an adult?
Yes. In an adult, contrast-enhanced CT is the most accurate test, with the highest sensitivity and specificity, and it shows abscess, perforation or an appendicolith.
Old PYQs expected ultrasound as the investigation of choice in general. Current practice uses ultrasound first only in children and pregnancy.

choices.label: Next: work through the adult case
Skip: I already know the adult test

say.text: Tempting: ultrasound is the test past papers keyed, so it feels like the answer. Ask who this patient is and what the test is most accurate for.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the old key against the adult rule before you rely on it again.

say.text: Ultrasound is first-line for children and pregnant women. For an adult, contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice and the most accurate test. The old key expected ultrasound in general, which is why it comes to mind.
Tempting: MRI is very accurate, so accuracy alone seems to decide. Which test does the pregnancy ladder put second, and what does that tell you about the first?

sure_note.text: You were sure accuracy alone picks the test. Check it against the ladder for pregnancy.

say.text: MRI without gadolinium is the second rung in pregnancy, used when ultrasound is inconclusive. In an adult, the investigation of choice is contrast-enhanced CT, the most accurate test.
Worked case. A 42-year-old man has right iliac fossa pain. Ultrasound was done and could not show the appendix.
Step 1: who is he? An adult, so the adult rule applies, with no child or pregnancy qualifier.
Step 2: an appendix you cannot see is not a normal one. Ultrasound calls it abnormal or normal only from a non-compressible, blind-ending tube over 6 mm.
Same 42-year-old man, scan still inconclusive. Step 3 is yours: what is your next step?

choices.label: Discharge, as the ultrasound has excluded appendicitis
Repeat the ultrasound in 6 hours, as it is most accurate
Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen now, as the adult next test
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Your scan did not show the appendix. Did it show it as normal, or did it fail to show it at all?
Yes. An inconclusive scan is not a negative one. Contrast-enhanced CT is the most accurate test in adults and shows abscess, perforation or an appendicolith.
Tempting: a scan feels final once it is done, and ultrasound is the first test you learned. Think about what this scan actually saw.

sure_note.text: You were sure a scan can rule it out. Check what this scan could and could not show.

say.text: A scan that cannot see the appendix does not show it normal. A negative result needs a visible, non-compressible tube over 6 mm. In an adult the test that settles it is contrast-enhanced CT, with the highest sensitivity and specificity.
Tempting: the old key taught ultrasound as the test of choice, so the most accurate-sounding test feels right. Ask whether that describes ultrasound in this adult.

sure_note.text: You were sure ultrasound is the most accurate test. Check that against the adult rule.

say.text: Ultrasound is first-line in children and pregnancy, not the most accurate test in adults. Contrast-enhanced CT is the investigation of choice for an adult. Repeating a scan that could not show the appendix will not change that.
A 6-year-old boy has right iliac fossa pain, fever and tenderness. Which first imaging do you order?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Read the age first. Does the first-line rule for a child match the adult answer you have just given?
Yes. In children, graded-compression ultrasound is first-line. It looks for a non-compressible, blind-ending tube over 6 mm.
Tempting: CT is the most accurate test, and you have just used it for an adult. Who is the patient in this stem?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read the age before the test. The adult answer is not the child's.

say.text: Tempting: a low-dose CT feels like a safer version of the adult test, so it looks like a compromise. Which test is first in a child, whatever the dose?

sure_note.text: You were sure a lower-dose CT is the child's answer. Check the first-line rule.

say.text: Ultrasound is the first-line test in children and pregnant women. Contrast-enhanced CT is the adult's most accurate test, and that rule does not carry over to a child.
A 24-year-old woman has right iliac fossa pain and irregular cycles. No pregnancy test has been done yet. What do you do first?

choices.label: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen, to settle the diagnosis
Diagnostic laparoscopy, as the appendix is the likely cause
Urine or serum beta-hCG, before any imaging or theatre
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what changes the whole plan in a woman of reproductive age, not only the appendix. Which test rules that out first?
Yes. Beta-hCG is done in every woman of reproductive age, because an ectopic pregnancy changes both the imaging and the surgery.
Tempting: CT is the test you would order for this pain, so it feels like the right first move. Which step comes before any test for the appendix?

sure_note.text: You were sure the scan comes first. In a woman of reproductive age the pregnancy test is first.

say.text: Tempting: a surgeon wants to go to the source and look. Does a diagnosis of the appendix come before excluding a pregnancy?

sure_note.text: You were sure theatre comes first. Check what must be excluded before any operation.

say.text: The pregnancy test comes first. Ectopic pregnancy, a ruptured ovarian cyst and pelvic inflammatory disease can mimic this picture, and each one changes the next step.
A 28-year-old woman, 20 weeks pregnant, has right iliac fossa pain and tenderness. Which first imaging do you order?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Pregnancy changes the first rung. Which test is the first rung in pregnancy, and which one comes next if that is inconclusive?
Yes. In pregnancy, graded-compression ultrasound is first. MRI without gadolinium is the next rung when ultrasound is inconclusive.
Tempting: MRI is accurate, so it feels like the best test for a pregnant woman. Which test is the first rung on the pregnancy ladder?

sure_note.text: You were sure MRI comes first. It is the second rung, not the first.

say.text: MRI without gadolinium is the second rung in pregnancy, used when ultrasound is inconclusive. The first rung is ultrasound, which is first-line in pregnancy.
Tempting: CT is the adult's most accurate test, so it feels right for any patient. Who is this patient, and what is her first test?

sure_note.text: You were sure CT is the answer for every patient. Read the qualifier before the test.

say.text: CT is the adult's most accurate test. In pregnancy and in children, ultrasound is first-line, so the pregnancy changes the first test, not the accuracy ranking.
Score this patient on Alvarado: migration of pain, right iliac fossa tenderness, rebound, fever and leucocytosis. What is the total?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Score each item once, at its weight in the table. Which items carry 2 points, and which carry 1?
Yes. Tenderness in the right iliac fossa and leucocytosis each score 2 points; the other items score 1. So 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 7.
Tempting: migration and rebound feel like strong signs, so they seem to deserve the 2-point weight. Check each item's weight against the table.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the weights. Recount each item against the table.

say.text: Tempting: leucocytosis is only a blood count, so it can seem like a minor item. Check the weight the table gives it.

sure_note.text: You were sure leucocytosis is a 1-point item. Check the table weight.

say.text: Migration and rebound score 1 each. A 9 comes from weighting both as 2. A 6 comes from scoring leucocytosis as 1, when it scores 2. The correct total is 7.
